rationale: Response A is better because it presents a cleaner factorial experiment—prompt-only, RAG, fine-tuning, and hybrid—and correctly identifies the RAG-to-hybrid delta as the key evidence for whether tuning adds value beyond retrieved knowledge. Its cost model is also more operationally complete, separating data curation, training, serving, maintenance, monitoring, and rollback, while its recommendations consistently distinguish changing facts from learned behavior. Response B has an excellent failure taxonomy and useful staleness and long-tail tests, but its training-data thresholds are internally inconsistent and several claims, especially its volume crossover and automatic freshness characterization, are too categorical. A also makes unsupported numerical crossover estimates and conflates on-premises compliance with fine-tuning somewhat, but overall it is more coherent, actionable, and directly tied to a defensible decision rule.
